newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portuguese crackdown does not solve TAP's problems.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese crackdown does not solve TAP's problems.

text.p: A Portuguese government decision to order striking pilots at state airline TAP-Air Portugal back to work has apparently failed to solve its immediate staff problems and could lead to more protests.

But, by ending the strike now, the government may have taken an initial step towards talks that will yield a long-term solution to the pilots' grievances over working hours, and help loss-making TAP to prepare for privatisation.

After an extraordinary cabinet meeting on Saturday afternoon, the government issued a special decree ordering pilots back to work to protect the public interest and safeguard jobs at the flag carrier.

TAP pilots had gone back on strike on Saturday, forcing the cancellation of three flights. The pilots decided on Thursday night to resume an indefinite strike, and were refusing to operate flights laid on at short notice.
Officials at the Civil Aviation Pilots' Union (SPAC), which represents all of TAP's 430 pilots, said they were consulting lawyers to verify that the government's decision was legal.
"SPAC will attack the government's decision if it is found to be illegal," one unidentified SPAC official told the Portuguese news agency Lusa on Saturday night.
"We regret that the government, which claims to be democratic, had to resort to force and coercion to resolve a labour dispute," the official added.
The pilots seemed to be backing down under government pressure for now because, under the decree, they will be liable to jail terms of between two and five years if they do not resume work.
But, if the union does find reason to have the decree declared illegal, the prospect of more disputes looms.

The decree does not resolve the pilots' complaints over working hours. The pilots say TAP employs too few of them, and that administrative staff often tell them at the last minute to change their work schedules, forcing them to fly after inadequate rest and jeopardising safety.

The government says it is doing all it can to satisfy the pilots' demands by pressing ahead with plans to invest 800 million escudos ($4.2 million) to upgrade the computer system which works out flight and work schedules.
The standoff has badly affected morale inside the airline, where ground staff have accused the pilots of putting the jobs of the airline's 7,500 employees at risk.
Both TAP's management and SPAC have said they were willing to continue talks. But relations have hit a low ebb since the state decree, and talks are likely to resume in a strained atmosphere.
Industry and political analysts say that TAP must resolve staff problems and improve its finances and marketing in order to become a viable prospect for privatisation.

"TAP must solve its staffing problems as a priority. It must also cut debt levels and improve its marketing. These steps are essential for TAP to appeal to investors in a privatisation," said Nigel Hawkins, transport analyst at brokerage Yamaichi International in London.
The government hopes to privatise TAP, at least partially, before the end of the century.
Government officials had warned that the strikes during the peak summer holiday season could point TAP towards bankruptcy.
Last April, TAP forecast that it could make a profit in 1997 for the first time in more than two decades. Estimates of the cost of the dispute were not immediately available.
The Portuguese state is barred by agreements with the European Union from pouring any more funds into the company.
The pilots began their protest two weekends ago, forcing TAP to cancel 12 flights and stranding at least 1,300 people.
The pilots then suspended the strike until Friday night to continue talks with management and government officials. After the talks failed, they voted overwhelmingly to resume the strike.
Last April TAP's pilots staged a two-day strike in a separate protest over working hours, grounding international flights and stranding 14,000 passengers. ($1=188.878 escudos)
